operations.evidence: Police use of force statistics are classified as official statistics.
Official-statistics status does not remove the documented recording and interpretation limitations.
The former experimental or official-statistics-in-development label was removed from the year ending March 2021 series.
The label change does not make force-level reporting perfectly comparable.
Police forces have been required to record the specified use-of-force data since April 2017.
The requirement does not guarantee every report is complete or consistently interpreted.
Forces submit use-of-force data to the Home Office through the Annual Data Requirement.
ADR submission is an administrative collection and not an independently observed event register.
The collection covers the 43 Home Office police forces and, voluntarily from the year ending March 2024, British Transport Police.
Coverage does not make local force systems or validation practices identical.
One report represents one officer's use of force on one person.
A single incident can generate several reports when several officers use force.
One report can include multiple tactics, reasons, impact factors, locations and outcomes.
Fields within one report must not be interpreted as one-to-one causal links.
Reports capture tactics, reasons, person characteristics, injuries, outcomes and location type.
The fields are officer-recorded and can contain missing or contradictory values.
The national collection excludes force used at designated public-order events where detailed individual reporting is not feasible.
The dataset is not a complete inventory of all force used by police.
Police forces choose their own systems for recording use-of-force data.
System differences can affect question wording, validation and field completeness.
Use-of-force reporting remains partly dependent on the reporting officer's judgement and interpretation.
Different officers at the same incident may record person or outcome details differently.
Home Office quality assurance checks whether submitted data are complete.
A completeness check cannot prove that every use of force was reported.
Home Office analysts query missing or contradictory values and work with forces on corrections.
Corrected administrative data can still contain residual error.
Each officer who uses force on an individual must complete a separate report for that person.
Report totals are not counts of unique people or unique incidents.
The collection cannot directly link an individual tactic to a reason, outcome, location or injury where multiple values are recorded.
A hospitalisation or injury field must not be attributed to a specific tactic without separate evidence.
Reported injuries or hospitalisation may pre-date or be unrelated to the officer's use of force.
Injury records are not medical causation findings.
A report may cover force used in more than one location.
A location category cannot establish where each tactic occurred or identify a parcel.
The national data cannot reliably provide details of a specific person or event.
The collection must not be used for exact-address attribution or individual prediction.
Counts are published unrounded and percentages use stated rounding rules.
Unrounded administrative counts still contain the inaccuracies inherent in large recording systems.
The latest Home Office publication incorporates revisions to previous data under its revisions policy.
Values should be versioned by release date and may change after force resubmission.
